title: WAFT: Warping-Alone Field Transforms for Optical Flow
claim: Replace an expensive cost-volume lookup with lightweight feature warping inside a simple recurrent loop to refine estimates iteratively.
layout: 2 dashed panels, left-to-right, recurrent ×T loop icon top-right
description: A two-part block diagram with dashed borders. The left panel, labeled 'Feature Extraction', stacks a photo of a small dog (Image), a dark-red trapezoid 'Input Encoder', and a gray rounded box 'Feature' below it. The right panel, labeled 'Feature-Space Warping and Iterative Updates', holds the main loop. A white box shows the flow field f_t, a purple dog silhouette on white. A gray 'Feature 2' box and the flow field feed into a circled 'W' warping node. That node's output goes into a large orange rounded box, 'Recurrent Update Module'. A gray 'Feature 1' box also feeds the update module from below. The module's output arrow leads to a second flow box, f_{t+1}. A circular-arrow icon with '× T' sits at the top-right corner to show iteration. Black arrows connect the boxes. The orange and red blocks draw the eye first.
caption: The meta-architecture of WAFT consists of an input encoder and a recurrent update module. We first extract image features from the input encoder, and then use these features to iteratively update the flow estimate for $T$ steps. At each step, we perform feature indexing through a lightweight backward warping on the feature of frame 2, removing the dependency on expensive cost volume used by previous work.
abstract: We introduce Warping-Alone Field Transforms (WAFT), a simple and effective method for optical flow. WAFT is similar to RAFT but replaces cost volume with high-resolution warping, achieving better accuracy with lower memory cost. This design challenges the conventional wisdom that constructing cost volumes is necessary for strong performance. WAFT is a simple and flexible meta-architecture with minimal inductive biases and reliance on custom designs. Compared with existing methods, WAFT ranks 1st on Spring, Sintel, and KITTI benchmarks, achieves the best zero-shot generalization on KITTI, while being 1.3-4.1x faster than existing methods that have competitive accuracy (e.g., 1.3x than Flowformer++, 4.1x than CCMR+). Code and model weights are available at \href{https://github.com/princeton-vl/WAFT}{https://github.com/princeton-vl/WAFT}.
